t: #4010 Maximize Pair Strength Using GCD — Direct Enumeration
o: Pick two elements a, b and maximize a·b/gcd(a,b)², i.e., the product of the coprime reduced parts. With [2,3,5] every pair is coprime so the answer is the largest product 15; with [4,6,8] the pair (6,8) reduces to (3,4) giving 12; with [3,3] it reduces to (1,1) giving 1. Since n ≤ 2000, there are under 2·10⁶ pairs — checking each with a gcd is easily fast enough.
k: Strength(a,b) = (a/g)·(b/g) where g = gcd(a,b) — always a positive integer.
n ≤ 2000 makes O(n² log V) brute force the intended solution; no structure is needed.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Pairs
a.i: Just evaluate the formula for every unordered pair and keep the maximum. Euclid's gcd costs O(log V) per pair.
s: Loop over all pairs i < j.
Compute g = gcd(nums[i], nums[j]) and the strength (nums[i]/g)*(nums[j]/g).
a.t: O(n² log V) — about 2·10⁶ pairs, each needing one Euclid gcd.

w: There is no meaningfully faster exact method worth coding at this size, so present the brute force confidently. Divide before multiplying (nums[i]/g * nums[j]/g) to avoid overflow; in Java/C++ use 64-bit intermediates since strengths can reach ~10¹⁰. Follow-ups: count pairs achieving the maximum, or handle up to 10⁵ elements (which would require grouping by gcd structure).
